title: Stop the invoice workers within a deploy's grace period

blocks.text: The invoice service takes invoice runs from a message broker and hands them to a worker pool. On a deploy the orchestrator gives the old process a grace period, then kills it. Two things go wrong today: runs that would have finished in a few seconds are cut off, and the runs that were waiting in the pool are simply lost, so customers miss their invoices until someone notices.
Write `stop(pool, grace, unit)` in `src/main/java/practice/Drain.java`, called by the deploy's shutdown hook:

items: work the pool already has, running or waiting, gets the grace period to finish, and `stop` returns only when it has finished or the grace period is over;
what is still running after the grace period is asked to stop, and gets one more grace period to do so; the runs that never started are returned, so the hook can put them back on the broker;
if the orchestrator interrupts the hook while `stop` waits, stop the pool at once, return what never started, and leave the hook's thread able to see that it was interrupted.

blocks.text: About twelve lines in total. The tests call `stop` on a thread of their own and use a pool with one worker.

cases.says: an idle pool stops, and nothing is handed back
invoice runs still waiting in the queue run to the end when they finish within the grace period
stop() does not return while an invoice run is still going and the grace period lasts
past the grace period the running invoice run is interrupted, and the runs that never started are handed back
a deployer interrupted while it waits stops the pool at once, hands back the queued runs, and keeps its interrupt flag

origin.section: shutdown() Stops Intake, Not Work: Wait for It With awaitTermination()

concepts: shutdown() refuses new tasks and returns at once while running and queued tasks still run; awaitTermination waits, and shutdownNow() is the fallback when it times out.
